scenes.tts: Where do the neurons of the cerebral cortex come from? In rodents, most come from one kind of cell.
scenes.visual: Title card fades. Question on screen: where do cortical neurons come from?
scenes.narration: Where do the neurons of the cerebral cortex come from? In rodents, most come from one kind of cell.

scenes.tts: Here is a slice through the wall of the embryonic mouse cortex. The ventricle, a fluid-filled space, is at the bottom.
scenes.visual: A vertical strip of embryonic mouse cortex draws in. Blue fluid band at the bottom labelled ventricle.
scenes.narration: Here is a slice through the wall of the embryonic mouse cortex. The ventricle, a fluid-filled space, is at the bottom.

scenes.tts: The surface facing the ventricle is apical. The outer surface, under the pia, is basal.
scenes.visual: Labels appear: apical (bottom edge, against the ventricle) and basal (top edge, under the pia). A thin line at the top labelled pia and basement membrane.
scenes.narration: The surface facing the ventricle is apical. The outer surface, under the pia, is basal.

scenes.tts: Beside the ventricle lies the ventricular zone, where progenitors live. A progenitor is a cell that still divides.
scenes.caption: Beside the ventricle lies the ventricular zone, where progenitors live. A progenitor is a cell that still divides.
scenes.visual: The lowest band shades and labels itself: ventricular zone (VZ). Definition card: progenitor = a cell that still divides.
scenes.narration: Beside the ventricle lies the ventricular zone, where progenitors live. A progenitor is a cell that still divides.

scenes.tts: Just outside it is the subventricular zone. Farther out, young neurons cross the intermediate zone to reach the cortical plate.
scenes.visual: Bands label upward in turn: subventricular zone (SVZ), intermediate zone, cortical plate, pia.
scenes.narration: Just outside it is the subventricular zone. Farther out, young neurons cross the intermediate zone to reach the cortical plate.

scenes.tts: Now light up one cell. It spans the whole wall.
scenes.visual: One long cell glows from the ventricle to the pia, crossing every band.
scenes.narration: Now light up one cell. It spans the whole wall.

scenes.tts: An apical foot sits on the ventricle. A long fibre ends in a basal foot under the pia.
scenes.visual: Callouts on the glowing cell: apical foot (bottom), long radial fibre, basal foot on the basement membrane (top).
scenes.narration: An apical foot sits on the ventricle. A long fibre ends in a basal foot under the pia.

scenes.tts: Early on, cells like this are neuroepithelial cells. As neurogenesis begins, in mouse around embryonic days ten to twelve, they become radial glia.
scenes.caption: Early on, cells like this are neuroepithelial cells. As neurogenesis begins, in mouse around embryonic days 10 to 12, they become radial glia.
scenes.visual: The cell's label changes from neuroepithelial cell to radial glial cell. Corner tag: mouse, about E10 to E12.
scenes.narration: Early on, cells like this are neuroepithelial cells. As neurogenesis begins, in mouse around embryonic days 10 to 12, they become radial glia.

scenes.tts: They keep the long shape. And they switch on proteins associated with glia.
scenes.visual: Small protein tags appear along the cell: GLAST, BLBP. Footnote: GFAP in primates.
scenes.narration: They keep the long shape. And they switch on proteins associated with glia.

scenes.tts: Look where cells divide. Most cells caught in mitosis sit against the ventricle. Cells copying their DNA sit farther out.
scenes.visual: A field of round mitotic cells glows along the ventricle. Higher in the VZ, nuclei glow a second colour, labelled copying DNA.
scenes.narration: Look where cells divide. Most cells caught in mitosis sit against the ventricle. Cells copying their DNA sit farther out.

scenes.tts: Two words will matter. A stem cell renews itself and makes more than one kind of cell.
scenes.visual: Definition card: stem cell = renews itself + makes more than one kind of cell.
scenes.narration: Two words will matter. A stem cell renews itself and makes more than one kind of cell.

scenes.tts: Radial glia, as a population, meet both conditions. An asymmetric division keeps one radial glial cell. Some single lineages later make glia as well as neurons.
scenes.visual: Two check marks appear on the card: keeps a radial glial cell; some lineages later make glia too (a minority, in mouse).
scenes.narration: Radial glia, as a population, meet both conditions. An asymmetric division keeps one radial glial cell. Some single lineages later make glia as well as neurons.

scenes.tts: And potential is not fate. Potential is what a cell can make alone in a dish. Fate is what it does make in the embryo.
scenes.visual: Split screen: a single cell in a dish labelled potential; the same cell in the embryo labelled fate.
scenes.narration: And potential is not fate. Potential is what a cell can make alone in a dish. Fate is what it does make in the embryo.

scenes.tts: Now the first puzzle. In fetal monkey cortex, young neurons climb radial glial fibres. Is the scaffold also the source of the neurons?
scenes.visual: A young neuron climbs the glowing fibre. Puzzle 1 card: scaffold or source?
scenes.narration: Now the first puzzle. In fetal monkey cortex, young neurons climb radial glial fibres. Is the scaffold also the source of the neurons?

scenes.tts: The second puzzle. Why does a progenitor copy its DNA out in the ventricular zone, then come back to the ventricle to divide?
scenes.visual: A nucleus rises within the VZ, glows for DNA copying, and sinks back to the ventricle. Puzzle 2 card: why divide at the ventricle?
scenes.narration: The second puzzle. Why does a progenitor copy its DNA out in the ventricular zone, then come back to the ventricle to divide?

scenes.tts: Here is the idea to carry through. A radial glial cell is a stem cell anchored at the ventricle.
scenes.visual: Idea card begins: a radial glial cell is a stem cell anchored at the ventricle.
scenes.narration: Here is the idea to carry through. A radial glial cell is a stem cell anchored at the ventricle.

scenes.tts: Each time it divides, it decides how many daughters stay radial glia.
scenes.visual: One radial glial cell divides; its two daughters are outlined, waiting to be sorted.
scenes.narration: Each time it divides, it decides how many daughters stay radial glia.

scenes.tts: Keep two, and its radial glial line doubles. Keep one, and the line holds steady while it makes neurons. Keep none, and its radial glial line ends.
scenes.visual: Three panels side by side: keep 2 (this line doubles), keep 1 (line steady, neuron made), keep 0 (radial glial line ends; a daughter may still divide).
scenes.narration: Keep two, and its radial glial line doubles. Keep one, and the line holds steady while it makes neurons. Keep none, and its radial glial line ends.

scenes.tts: A daughter that leaves is spent as a stem cell. It becomes a neuron, or an intermediate progenitor that usually makes two.
scenes.visual: A leaving daughter branches two ways: one neuron; or an intermediate progenitor that splits, usually into two neurons.
scenes.narration: A daughter that leaves is spent as a stem cell. It becomes a neuron, or an intermediate progenitor that usually makes two.

scenes.tts: Count those choices round by round, and you can see how the number of neurons depends on them.
scenes.visual: A tally counter beside the cell ticks up as divisions repeat. Corner tag: simple counting model, no cell death.
scenes.narration: Count those choices round by round, and you can see how the number of neurons depends on them.

scenes.tts: This is a counting model, for projection neurons of rodent dorsal cortex. Outer radial glia, common in primates, renew themselves without the anchor.
scenes.visual: Scope card: counting model; excitatory projection neurons, rodent dorsal cortex; no cell death. Side note: outer radial glia, no apical contact.
scenes.narration: This is a counting model, for projection neurons of rodent dorsal cortex. Outer radial glia, common in primates, renew themselves without the anchor.

scenes.tts: And the rule counts. It does not explain what makes a daughter stay or leave.
scenes.visual: Scope card adds: counts, does not explain. Arrow points to later lessons: Notch, asymmetric division.
scenes.narration: And the rule counts. It does not explain what makes a daughter stay or leave.

scenes.tts: So hold on to one picture. One long cell across the wall, spending its divisions one choice at a time.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card over the glowing cell: one cell across the wall, spending its divisions one choice at a time.
scenes.narration: So hold on to one picture. One long cell across the wall, spending its divisions one choice at a time.
